newsitem.title: HUNGARY: Ciorbea visit to cement Hungary, Romania ties.
newsitem.headline: Ciorbea visit to cement Hungary, Romania ties.

text.p: Romanian Prime Minister Victor Ciorbea visits Hungary this week as both countries put years of strained relations behind them and Romania tries to link its bid to join NATO with that of Hungary.

Ciorbea, who arrives on Wednesday, is the first Romanian premier to visit Hungary since communism collapsed in 1989. The prime minister, whose centre-right coalition took over from leftists in November, told Hungarian media it is no accident he chose Hungary for his first official trip abroad.

"It is absolutely not by chance, it is instead proof of how important we regard our bilateral relations and what enormous importance we give to the active partnership between Hungary and Romania," Ciorbea told the daily Nepszabadsag.
"We are interested in relations with Hungary not just as a good neighbour but in an active partnership in political, economic and even military relations," Ciorbea said.
Hungarian and Romanian analysts say the significance of Ciorbea's visit, and an earlier trip to Hungary by Romania's new Foreign Minister Adrian Severin, cannot be overstated.

"They didn't go to Germany or France or even the United States but to Hungary," said Laszlo Valki, professor of international law at Hungary's Eotvos University. "It is an unequivocal sign of their priorities."
High on the list for discussions, diplomats and officials said, are linkage of the Hungarian and Romanian bids to join NATO and Hungarian investment in Romania's struggling economy.

Ciorbea will meet businessmen at one of Hungary's top restaurants and will visit Szekesfehervar, the western Hungarian "economic miracle" town that is host to subsidiaries of major companies such as IBM and Philips.
Bilateral trade is "very, very small" Valki said, but could expand significantly if Hungary did more business with Romania's 1.6-million ethnic Hungarian minority.
Hungary, along with Poland and the Czech Republic, is deemed a front-runner for first-round enlargement of NATO, to be decided at a summit in Madrid in July.

Romania could not have hoped to make the list under its previous government, analysts said. But since the centre-right coalition ousted leftist president Ion Iliescu, Romania and Hungary have rapidly signed agreements to form a joint military battalion, open more border crossings and reopen and establish new consulates.

Hungarian Foreign Minister Laszlo Kovacs, after meetings in Washington last week with U.S. Secretary of State Madeleine Albright and other officials, said Romania is lobbying hard for inclusion in the first round, and Hungary backs its bid.

"I expressed the view that simultaneous accession could be achieved certainly not by slowing down accession of Hungary, but by accelerating the accession of Romania, and we give full support to it," Kovacs told a news conference upon his return.

Such statements denote a sharp change in relations from seven years ago when four people were killed and hundreds injured during inter-ethnic clashes in Tirgu Mures in Romania's ethnic-Hungarian heartland of Transylvania.
Romanian nationalists allied with then-president Iliescu accused Budapest of harbouring designs on the central Transylvania region, ruled by Austria-Hungary until 1918.
Bilateral ties improved only slowly under Iliescu until Romania and Hungary signed a friendship treaty last year.
"What is happening today is a normal evolution based on the clear and clean political will proved by the two governments," Ioan Donca, Romanian ambassador to Hungary, told Reuters.

But western diplomats and analysts said it was Ciorbea's decision to name ethnic Hungarians for the first time as ministers of ethnic minority affairs and tourism that greatly accelerated the process of defusing tensions.

"Now you have a situation where the Romanian opposition (Iliescu's backers) can't complain about the friendship treaty they signed and the opposition in Hungary can't criticise a Romanian government that includes ethnic Hungarians," a diplomat said.
"That's the key. There is a lot more to Hungarian-Romanian relations than the ethnic issue, but it is the keystone."
